title: OpenAI published BioBasicsBench on 6 November. At the xhigh setting GPT-6 Astra scores 66.7 percent on 100 wet-lab tasks, against 43.8 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol. The post says a higher score is not yet a reliable lab judgment. Anthropic’s engineering post the same day describes dreaming, an offline pass that checks memory notes against transcripts. On one Pokémon run, Fable 5 kept a small folder and earned four badges. Sonnet 3.7 kept 413 files and earned one. Meta is rolling out unnamed models, trained using Muse Wonder, to Muse and Meta AI. Its memory eval is 90 percent, from 76. A separate sentence says forgetting fell 2.4 times. Pushmeet Kohli wrote that two weaknesses are in legacy 1024-bit RSA, and that they do not affect schemes such as RSA 2048. Bloomberg, carried by FA Mag, says buyers are discussing $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion. One person weighed $1.1 trillion. Anthropic declined to comment. The Frontier Model Forum’s jailbreak scale is Version 1.0, posted 5 November. It says it does not estimate harm.
summary: On Friday 6 November 2026 OpenAI published BioBasicsBench, 100 routine wet-lab tasks built with Ligo. At xhigh, GPT-6 Astra averages 66.7 percent of the available credit, interval 60.3 to 73.1, against 43.8 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol, interval 37.6 to 50.0. The post says it ran 18,500 results and that a higher score is not yet a reliable judgment in the lab. On one plate it says Astra’s colony count was about 12 percent high. The same day Anthropic’s engineering post, by Lance Martin, described how Claude writes memory and how dreaming can correct it. The Pokémon comparison is one run of each model at about 10,000 steps. A Stainless corpus of about 350,000 files went from 13 percent to 48 percent of graded criteria on 25 questions as dreaming scaled from two sessions to 128. Meta’s research post the same day says specialized versions of existing models, trained using Muse Wonder, are rolling out to Muse and Meta AI. It does not name them. The Personal Superintelligence Index on the page is 47 percent, from 38. The Active Memory eval is 90 percent, from 76. The 2.4 times line, and the 67 percent line, are different sentences. Pushmeet Kohli posted that human-guided agents made two advances against legacy 1024-bit RSA, on older signatures and on factoring keys in bulk, and that the results do not affect modern schemes such as RSA 2048. This edition used that post, not a paper. FA Mag’s 6 November article, provided by Bloomberg News, says people familiar are discussing a $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion range ahead of formal marketing next week, that one of them weighed $1.1 trillion, and that Anthropic declined to comment. The Nasdaq 100 line in the article is a 6.4 percent drop on Thursday and $2.3 trillion of market value. The Frontier Model Forum posted Version 1.0 of a cyber jailbreak rating framework on 5 November. The specification says the bands are Negligible, Low, Medium, High or Critical, that the scale is not a harm estimate, and that it is not operational guidance yet. Comments run through 21 December 2026.
uncertainty: The 66.7 percent, 43.8 percent, 62.0 percent, 38.3 percent, 35.4 percent, 33.2 percent and 31.2 percent are OpenAI’s xhigh means, with the intervals and token counts printed in the same table. Xhigh is the highest setting the post reports for all seven models. The 18,500 is the post’s total across 37 settings, five attempts and 100 tasks. This edition did not add the rows, and it did not test whether two intervals overlap. The kind-of-data counts overlap, which the post says, so they are not a sum of 100. Approximately 12 percent is the post’s net overcount on one plate. The lanes and the antibiotic label are examples in the post, not a rate. Anthropic’s Pokémon figures are one run of Sonnet 3.7 and one run of Fable 5, at about 10,000 steps. Nine files in two folders, plus global.md, and 413 files across 225 folders, are those runs. Four badges and one badge are those runs. Opus 5.5 beating the game is a separate sentence. The 13 percent and 48 percent are graded criteria on 25 questions about a Stainless corpus of about 350,000 files and roughly 420 million tokens, from two dreaming sessions to 128. The 54 percent, 61 percent and 53 percent are search-plus-wiki against search alone, and 48 percent is the best wiki-only score in that passage. About 20,000 tokens is the post’s saving per question. The 87 percent and 73 percent are the red and orange items in a set of 24 merger questions, not all 24. The 41 of 57, the 72 percent, and the later 57 of 57 are the contract-terms test before and after the instructions changed. Nine out of ten, and less than half, are how often Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 4.6 read memory on that test. Nearly doubled is the post’s description of a prompt on Sonnet 4.6, not a score this edition calculated. The 200 lines and 25 KB are what Claude Code loads from MEMORY.md. The Managed Agents docs, as read for this edition, call dreaming a research preview. Meta’s 47, 38, 90, 76, 2.4 times and 67 percent are Meta’s. The post does not define the index, does not give the 67 percent a baseline, and does not name the models. This edition did not turn 90 and 76 into 2.4. Kohli’s 6 November post is the source for the two RSA advances and for RSA 2048. This edition did not read the essay he linked, and it did not use multipliers that appeared in other people’s posts. The $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion range is people familiar, via Bloomberg, as carried by FA Mag on 6 November. $1.1 trillion is one of those people. $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion is what the article says Bloomberg had previously reported. The 6.4 percent and $2.3 trillion are the article’s account of the Nasdaq 100 on Thursday. Anthropic declined to comment. No final decision is in the article. The jailbreak framework is dated 5 November. The bands, the October 2026 baseline, and the line that a score of 0 is not a clean bill of health are the specification. Comments to comments@frontiermodelforum.org run through 21 December 2026. Feedback from NIST, the NSA, and two UK bodies does not, the page says, imply endorsement. stories.theme: BioBasicsBench puts GPT-6 Astra at 66.7 percent. The post says that is not a lab judgment yet
stories.changed: On Friday 6 November 2026 OpenAI published “Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science.” The post introduces BioBasicsBench, developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design. It says the benchmark has 100 tasks drawn from scientists’ own experiments, across five areas: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Tasks run from reading a molecular weight on a gel to a detailed assay. Each task has an expert-written rubric. The post says each one was reviewed by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, then by an external PhD-level scientist working in a wet lab, then again inside Ligo. Agents return a conclusion, a measurement or a recommendation, and get credit criterion by criterion, so a right answer can still lose points on the reasoning. At the xhigh setting, which the post says allows more reasoning per task, GPT-6 Astra earned an average of 66.7 percent of the available credit, compared with 43.8 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol. The same table prints a 95 percent confidence interval of 60.3 to 73.1 percent for Astra and 37.6 to 50.0 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 4,704 output tokens per task against 9,099. The post says it tested seven models over 37 model and reasoning-effort settings, five attempts on each of the 100 tasks, for a total of 18,500 results. On that xhigh table the other rows are GPT-6.1 Sol at 62.0 percent (55.6 to 68.4 percent, 5,238 tokens), GPT-6 Luna at 38.3 percent (32.3 to 44.5, 13,120 tokens), GPT-5.5 at 35.4 percent (29.7 to 41.0, 11,135), GPT-5.4 at 33.2 percent (28.3 to 38.4, 13,717) and GPT-5.2 at 31.2 percent (26.2 to 36.3, 27,620). The post says a task can include several kinds of data, and that those counts overlap. It lists gels and blots on 31 tasks, protocols, notes and specs on 27, tables and instrument exports on 20, bench photos on 18, microscopy on 14, instrument screens on 13, sequencing files on 12, protocol videos on 7, agar plates on 7, and reference sheets, which it calls supporting material, on 21. The post says GPT-6 Astra substantially improves on GPT-5.6 Sol. Its comparison sentence is that pair. It also says higher benchmark scores do not yet mean models can make reliable judgments in the lab. In one example Astra proposes colony lanes 4, 6, 7 and 8 where the reference selects 5, 9 and 10. In another it treats a plate labeled for a different antibiotic as a control. On one counting plate the post says the net result is an overcount of approximately 12 percent relative to the reference, and that with the plated volume and dilution held fixed an overcount inflates the efficiency estimate by the same proportion. This edition did not rerun the tasks.
stories.matters: 66.7 percent is a mean on 100 routine tasks, at one reasoning setting, from the lab that made the model. The post’s next section is the model still calling the wrong colonies and counting one plate high.
stories.imply: Do not tell a lab that an agent can now sign off a gel. The post says a higher score is not a reliable judgment. Do not tell them Astra beat GPT-6.1 Sol. The post’s comparison sentence is with GPT-5.6 Sol. The table also prints 62.0 percent for GPT-6.1 Sol. This edition did not test the intervals.
uses: If a slide needs the headline, use the pair the post prints. At xhigh, 66.7 percent of the available credit for GPT-6 Astra, 43.8 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol, on 100 tasks, five attempts each. Put the intervals beside them: 60.3 to 73.1, and 37.6 to 50.0.

Keep the 12 percent in its own sentence. It is the post’s net overcount on one colony plate, not the benchmark mean. The post says that kind of miss inflates an efficiency estimate when volume and dilution stay fixed.
The 18,500 is the post’s total across 37 settings. It is not a count of tasks. The data-type counts overlap, which the post says, so they do not add up to 100.
stories.example: A science lead asked whether an agent can call the colonies on a cloning plate reads the 6 November post past the 66.7. That figure is the xhigh mean. In the post’s own cloning example, Astra picks lanes 4, 6, 7 and 8 and the reference picks 5, 9 and 10. The post says the higher score is not yet a reliable lab judgment.
stories.audience: Anyone who would hand a gel, a plate photo or a protocol video to an agent, and anyone who has to say what 66.7 percent is.
stories.watch: Whether a lab that did not write the tasks reruns the 100. Whether a later note prices the tokens or says who may see the images. No new chat model shipped with the benchmark. GPT-6 Astra was already the model named in the table.

source.title: OpenAI: BioBasicsBench, 6 November 2026
source.quote: At the ‘xhigh’ setting, which allows more reasoning per task, GPT-6 Astra earned an average of 66.7% of the available credit, compared with 43.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol.

stories.theme: Dreaming checks Claude’s notes against the transcript. One small folder is not a score
stories.changed: On Friday 6 November 2026 Anthropic published “The components of agent memory,” by Lance Martin, from the engineering team. The post says agent memory is knowledge Claude keeps between sessions, as notes it can read later. It says that excludes a change to the weights, learning inside one conversation, and compaction. Dreaming, as the post describes it, is an offline pass over logs. It can correct a note, write new notes, build a wiki, or choose what gets loaded at the start of the next session. The post compares one Pokémon run of Claude Sonnet 3.7 with one run of Claude Fable 5, each at about 10,000 steps, with a folder the model could read and write. Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge. Fable 5 wrote nine files in two folders, plus a top-level file called global.md, and earned four badges. Around step 10,000, Sonnet 3.7 spent the next 17 steps creating six files and deleting nine, and took no actions in the game. The post says Fable 5 progressed further with the smaller folder, and that Opus 5.5 kept a small folder of the current goal and beat the game. On a separate test, the post says Sonnet 5 read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times, and Sonnet 4.6 did so less than half the time. Prompting Sonnet 4.6 to read the files and test its theories nearly doubled its score on that task. The post does not print the two scores. Dreaming’s correction example is one wrong note: Claude had written that a PokéCenter was on the east side of Mt. Moon. Checked against the transcript, the note was rewritten. With the corrected note, that run went back into the cave and reached Cerulean City. With the uncorrected note, Claude dropped back onto the earlier route three times and the run ended without reaching Cerulean City. The post also built wikis over an internal Stainless corpus of about 350,000 files, roughly 420 million tokens. On 25 questions, scores grew from 13 percent to 48 percent of graded criteria as dreaming scaled from two sessions to 128. With search and the wiki, the aggregate score rose from 54 percent to 61 percent, against 53 percent for search alone. The best wiki-only score in that passage is 48 percent. The post says search plus the wiki also saved about 20,000 tokens per question. On 24 questions about a merger, more than half of which needed several documents, the post says Claude scored 87 percent on the items that needed several documents or a judgment when it used the wiki, against 73 percent with search alone. On one contract test, a shared table kept 41 of 57 facts, which the post calls 72 percent. After the instructions gave each contract its own page, 57 of 57 facts survived, and the post says 100 percent of the criteria could be met, up from 72 percent. Claude Code, the post says, loads only the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY.md. The Managed Agents docs, as read for this edition, call dreaming a research preview and say to request access. The engineering post does not say every Claude seat runs that job.
stories.matters: A note written in the session can be wrong, and the next session can trust it. Dreaming is the post’s way of checking the note against the transcript. The badge counts are one run each.
stories.imply: Do not tell a team that fewer memory files produce more progress. The post shows one run of two models. Do not quote 48 percent as a general memory score. It is 25 questions on one corpus, after 128 dreaming sessions. Do not say dreaming is on for every customer. The docs call the Managed Agents feature a research preview.
uses: If someone cites the Pokémon result, keep the design in the sentence. One run each, about 10,000 steps. Sonnet 3.7: 413 files, 225 folders, one badge. Fable 5: nine files in two folders, plus global.md, four badges. The post says the smaller folder went further. It does not print a second run.

Keep the Stainless numbers together. About 350,000 files. 25 questions. 13 percent to 48 percent of graded criteria, from two sessions to 128. Search plus the wiki, 54 percent to 61 percent, against 53 percent for search alone. About 20,000 tokens saved per question.
The line a coding team can check today is Claude Code’s. The post says auto memory loads the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY.md, and that a longer instruction file is a weaker one.
stories.example: A team asked whether to let an agent keep a file for every decision opens the 6 November post at the Pokémon runs. The model that wrote 413 files spent 17 steps on the folder and took no action in the game. The post’s other point is the wrong PokéCenter note: until dreaming checked it against the transcript, a later session treated the east side as true.
stories.audience: Anyone whose coding agent writes notes for the next session, and anyone about to treat a memory score as a product benchmark.
stories.watch: Whether the research preview becomes a control a customer can turn on, and what it costs. Whether a second Pokémon run is published. The post does not name a new Claude model.

source.title: Anthropic: The components of agent memory, 6 November 2026
source.quote: As we scaled dreaming from two sessions to 128, performance on the 25 questions grew from 13% to 48% of graded criteria.

stories.theme: Meta’s Muse update is an unnamed model. 90 percent and 2.4 times are different sentences
stories.changed: On Friday 6 November 2026 Meta AI published “Bringing Specialized Models to Muse and Meta AI.” The post says specialized versions of existing models, trained using Muse Wonder, are rolling out to people who use Muse and Meta AI. It does not name the models. It says Muse Wonder remains the frontier series introduced a few weeks earlier, and that these are specialized versions of the models already behind Muse and Meta AI. The page prints a Personal Superintelligence Index of 47 percent for the current Muse model and 38 percent for the previous one. It does not say what the index is made of. It says Active Memory and Active Focus, which it introduced with Muse Wonder, are coming to these specialized models. Active Memory, it says, is meant to tell temporary information from permanent information, and current information from stale information. The example in that section is a 2.4 times reduction, in Muse, in forgetting critical information necessary for a goal. A chart on the same page is a different pair. It says the current Muse model uses critical context correctly on 90 percent of Active Memory eval tasks, and the previous model on 76 percent. Active Focus, the post says, is training on bottlenecks so the model can try again, recover, or find another way. In Muse, it says, the models show a 67 percent improvement in completing everyday tasks where unexpected issues arise. It does not print the baseline that 67 percent improves on. It says the models were also trained to switch between pushing a goal alone and working live with the person, and to take a correction in the middle of a task. In Meta AI, it says the same changes help with steps, follow-up questions, and a change of direction. The post does not say Wonder itself is now the model in the free apps.
stories.matters: The number a product manager can repeat is 90 percent against 76 percent, on Meta’s Active Memory eval. The 2.4 times line is about forgetting. The post does not show the arithmetic that would make them the same figure.
stories.imply: Do not write that Muse is now 2.4 times better, or that the index moved from 76 to 90. Those are three sentences. Do not name a model the post does not name. Do not tell a team that every seat now runs Muse Wonder. The post says specialized versions of existing models are rolling out to Muse and Meta AI.
uses: Keep three figures in three sentences. Index: 47 percent, from 38, and the post does not define the index. Active Memory eval: 90 percent of tasks using critical context, from 76. Forgetting: a 2.4 times reduction, in Muse, of critical information for a goal.
The 67 percent needs the missing baseline in the same sentence. The post says a 67 percent improvement on everyday tasks where something unexpected happens. It does not say 67 percent of what.
The access line is the first paragraph. Specialized versions, trained using Muse Wonder, rolling out to Muse and Meta AI. Not a new public model name.
stories.example: A workplace admin asked whether Friday’s Muse update is Muse Wonder for every seat reads the noun in the post. It says specialized versions of existing models, trained using Muse Wonder. The 90 percent is Meta’s eval of using critical context. The 2.4 times is a different sentence, about forgetting.
stories.audience: Anyone who administers Muse or Meta AI, and anyone who might put 2.4 times and 90 percent on the same slide as one result.
stories.watch: Whether Meta names the models or publishes the index. Whether the 67 percent gets a baseline. The post does not say a Wonder price changed.

source.title: Meta AI: Specialized models for Muse and Meta AI, 6 November 2026
source.quote: For example, our improved models in Muse show a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information necessary for helping you achieve your goals.

stories.theme: Kohli says two weaknesses are in legacy 1024-bit RSA. He says RSA 2048 is not those results
stories.changed: On Friday 6 November 2026 Pushmeet Kohli, vice president of science at Google DeepMind, posted that the DeepMind science team was sharing two cryptographic advances against legacy 1024-bit RSA. The post says the team worked with cryptanalysis experts and that AI agents made the two advances in just weeks. It says the results can bypass older digital signature protections and can factor legacy 1024-bit RSA keys in bulk. It says these results do not affect the security of modern encryption schemes such as RSA 2048. It says the results are a reason not to assume the mathematical hardness of schemes relied on in the past, and that AI can help defenders improve standards ahead of future threats. The same post points to a longer essay on X, titled “Advancing the frontier of cryptanalysis.” Google DeepMind’s account, a few minutes later, said that guided by humans, the models uncovered two major weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems. This edition used Kohli’s post. It did not read a paper, and it did not use speed-ups that other accounts attached to the news.
stories.matters: The sentence a security lead can use is the bound. Legacy 1024-bit RSA, not a break of RSA 2048. The post does not name a live system.
stories.imply: Do not tell a board that DeepMind broke modern RSA. Kohli’s sentence names RSA 2048 as a scheme these results do not affect. Do not quote a multiplier for the speed-up. This edition did not find that number in his post. Do not call the agents unsupervised. Both posts say people guided the work.
uses: Write the status as one sentence. On 6 November 2026 Kohli said two advances, made with cryptanalysis experts in just weeks, apply to legacy 1024-bit RSA: older signature protections, and factoring keys in bulk. He said they do not affect schemes such as RSA 2048.
The workplace check is an inventory, not a new control. Anything still offering a 1024-bit RSA key is the generation his post is about. A 2048-bit key is outside the sentence he wrote.
If a slide adds a factor of 30 or 1,600, take it off. Those figures were not in the post this edition used.
stories.example: A security lead asked whether Friday’s DeepMind post means their TLS certificates are exposed reads the key size in Kohli’s sentence. The weaknesses he describes are in legacy 1024-bit RSA. He writes that the results do not affect modern schemes such as RSA 2048. The post does not name a vendor or a live incident.
stories.audience: Anyone who still has a 1024-bit RSA key in a certificate, a device or a partner API, and anyone who might brief the result as a break of current encryption.
stories.watch: Whether the essay he linked is followed by a paper that prints the method and the cost. Whether a standards body names a migration date. No new Gemini model shipped with the post.

source.title: Pushmeet Kohli, Google DeepMind, 6 November 2026
source.quote: While these results do not affect the security of modern encryption schemes  such as RSA 2048, these results show why we must not assume the mathematical "hardness" of cryptographic schemes which we have relied upon in the past.

stories.theme: Bloomberg says buyers are discussing $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion. One person said $1.1 trillion
stories.changed: FA Mag, in an article dated 6 November 2026 and provided by Bloomberg News, said Anthropic’s IPO plans ran into a post-election selloff and that prospective investors are rethinking the valuation. The article says that ahead of formal IPO marketing next week, potential buyers are discussing a $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion range, according to people familiar with the matter. It says some are weighing a value as low as $1.1 trillion, and that this $1.1 trillion is one of those people. It says investors had previously told bankers their estimate of a fair valuation had moved to about $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion, which Bloomberg had reported, and that the estimate shifted again after the Nasdaq 100 plunged 6.4 percent on Thursday, wiping out $2.3 trillion of market value, a record for a single day. It says deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions have been made. It says a spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment. It says investors had estimated a fair value as high as $2 trillion in early October, and that the retreat to $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion followed an October briefing on the latest financials. It says a delay is another, less palatable option, not a decision the company has announced. Max Kettner of HSBC, quoted from Bloomberg Radio, said around $1 trillion could be a more comfortable level. That is his view. It is not a bid in the $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion sentence. Reuters, the day before, had reported that some potential investors saw a discussed $1.5 trillion as the high end. This article is a later, lower band, from different unnamed people. It does not say the roadshow has been cancelled.
stories.matters: $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion is a discussion Bloomberg attributes to people familiar. $1.1 trillion is one person. Anthropic did not confirm either number on 6 November.
stories.imply: Do not put $1.1 trillion on a slide as the valuation. It is one unnamed person’s weighing, inside a reported range, and the company declined to comment. Do not say the listing has slipped. The article still frames formal marketing as next week, and it says no final decision has been made. Do not mix this range with Reuters’s $1.5 trillion sentence from 5 November. That was a different report.
uses: Keep the attributions in separate sentences. People familiar, via Bloomberg: a $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion discussion. One of them: as low as $1.1 trillion. Anthropic: declined to comment. Kettner: around $1 trillion would be more comfortable, which is a strategist’s comment, not the range.
The 6.4 percent and the $2.3 trillion are the article’s account of the Nasdaq 100 on Thursday. They are not a figure Anthropic printed.
The $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion is what the article says buyers had told bankers before Thursday, and what it says Bloomberg had already reported. It is not this article’s new range.
stories.example: A treasurer asked whether Anthropic is now a $1.1 trillion IPO reads the verb in the FA Mag copy. Potential buyers are discussing $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, people familiar told Bloomberg. One of them is weighing $1.1 trillion. Anthropic declined to comment. The copy does not say a range has been set.
stories.audience: Anyone who has to say what Anthropic’s discussed valuation is after Thursday’s market drop, and whether that replaced the $1.5 trillion line from 5 November.
stories.watch: Whether a bank or Anthropic names a range. Whether the $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion discussion moves again before marketing. The article does not say a model changed.

source.title: Bloomberg, via FA Mag: Anthropic IPO valuation talk, 6 November 2026
source.quote: A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment.

stories.theme: The Forum’s jailbreak scale is Version 1.0. It says it is not a harm estimate, and not for operations yet
stories.changed: On Thursday 5 November 2026 the Frontier Model Forum posted Version 1.0 of a Jailbreak Rating Framework for Frontier Cyber Threats. The specification says it rates one successful jailbreak against one frontier model, and that a successful jailbreak is a reproducible method, such as a prompt, a template, a multi-turn procedure or a harness, that bypasses that version’s safeguards. It scores four categories: capability gain, capability scope, ease of deployment, and ease of discovery. It says those resolve into a severity and a likelihood, then into one band: Negligible, Low, Medium, High or Critical. It says the band does not prescribe a response. It says the framework measures relative risk, supports comparisons, and is not intended to estimate the actual harm a jailbreak could cause. It says the dimensions, tiers and thresholds are a starting point for discussion rather than guidance to apply operationally. It says a score of 0 on a frontier-risk dimension does not mean the behavior is acceptable. It means the case is below the frontier bar and belongs to ordinary risk management. If capability gain is 0, it says, stop and call the case Negligible. The baseline it names is the most cyber-capable widely available models as of the assessment date, currently October 2026. It says ExploitBench and ExploitGym are reasonable initial screens and will likely need replacing when they saturate. It says the same jailbreak, unchanged, scores differently when the baseline moves. Comments go to comments@frontiermodelforum.org through 21 December 2026. The page thanks experts from NIST CAISSI, NSA SISC, UK AISI and UK NCSC, and says feedback does not imply endorsement. The introductory post the same day quotes Sasha Baker, OpenAI’s head of national security policy, calling the framework a step toward a common methodology. OpenAI’s account on X posted about that partnership on 6 November. That post is not a second version of the document.
stories.matters: A security team can use the four categories as a shared vocabulary. The specification says not to treat the band as the harm, and not to run the scale operationally until it has been tested on more jailbreaks.
stories.imply: Do not file a Critical band as a measurement of damage. The page says the band is not a harm estimate and does not tell a company what to patch first. Do not tell an auditor the UK or US bodies endorsed it. The page says their feedback is not an endorsement. Do not date the document 6 November. The specification is 5 November. OpenAI’s post the next day points at it.
uses: Write the status as Version 1.0, posted 5 November 2026, open for comment through 21 December. Four categories. Five bands. Not operational guidance, which is the specification’s line.

If a finding is scored, keep the model version in the sentence. The unit is one reproducible jailbreak against one specified model. A score of 0 is not, the page says, a statement that the behavior is fine.
The October 2026 baseline is the page’s. It names ExploitGym as a screen that will go stale. It does not reprint a model’s ExploitGym score.
stories.example: A security lead asked whether a jailbreak labeled Critical is a severity they can put in an incident ticket reads the specification’s limit. The band compares one reproducible bypass with others. The page says it does not estimate the harm, and that companies still decide the response. Comments on the scale itself are open through 21 December.
stories.audience: Anyone who triages jailbreaks across more than one lab, and anyone who might treat a forum band as a regulatory score.
stories.watch: Whether a later version says different assessors reach the same band. The page says that test is still to be done. Whether the 21 December comments change a threshold. No model shipped with the framework.

source.title: Frontier Model Forum: Jailbreak Rating Framework, Version 1.0, 5 November 2026
source.quote: It supports comparisons between findings, but is not intended to estimate the actual harm a given jailbreak could cause, which depends on additional factors outside the scope of this framework.

signals.raw: OpenAI, 6 Nov: BioBasicsBench, 100 wet-lab tasks with Ligo. At xhigh, GPT-6 Astra 66.7 percent of available credit, interval 60.3 to 73.1, against 43.8 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol, interval 37.6 to 50.0. GPT-6.1 Sol on the same table is 62.0 percent. 18,500 results across 37 settings. One plate overcounted by about 12 percent. The post says a higher score is not yet a reliable lab judgment. Not a new chat model.

Anthropic engineering, 6 Nov: dreaming checks memory notes against transcripts. One Pokémon run each at about 10,000 steps. Sonnet 3.7: 413 files, 225 folders, one badge. Fable 5: nine files in two folders plus global.md, four badges. Stainless: about 350,000 files, 25 questions, 13 percent to 48 percent of criteria from two sessions to 128. Claude Code loads the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY.md. Managed Agents docs call dreaming a research preview. Not a new model.

Meta, 6 Nov: specialized versions of existing models, trained using Muse Wonder, rolling out to Muse and Meta AI. Unnamed. Index 47 percent from 38, index undefined in the post. Active Memory eval 90 percent from 76. A separate sentence: 2.4 times less forgetting of critical information. 67 percent improvement with no baseline printed. Not Muse Wonder for every seat.

Pushmeet Kohli, 6 Nov: two advances against legacy 1024-bit RSA, with cryptanalysis experts, in just weeks. Older signature protections, and factoring keys in bulk. He says the results do not affect modern schemes such as RSA 2048. Guided by humans. This edition did not read the essay and did not use other accounts’ multipliers. Not a new model.

Bloomberg via FA Mag, 6 Nov: people familiar discuss a $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion range ahead of marketing next week. One person weighed $1.1 trillion. Anthropic declined to comment. Nasdaq 100 down 6.4 percent on Thursday, $2.3 trillion of value, as the article states it. No final decision. Not a cancellation of the roadshow, and not a new model.

Frontier Model Forum, 5 Nov: Jailbreak Rating Framework Version 1.0. Four categories, bands from Negligible to Critical. Not a harm estimate. Not operational guidance. A score of 0 is not a clean bill of health. Baseline is October 2026. Comments through 21 December. OpenAI’s account pointed at it on 6 Nov. Not a new model.
